problem: Source says 'bring back to his home and his peers'; candidate adds 'family' ('bring home to his family and his peers'), an addition.
replacement: Among aristocratic nations, especially those where birth is the only source of rank, the army has the same inequality as the nation. The officer is a noble and the soldier a serf; the first is naturally called to command and the second to obey. In aristocratic armies, then, the ordinary soldier’s ambition is held within very narrow limits. The officer’s ambition has no unlimited range either. An aristocratic body is not only one step on the nation’s ladder of ranks; it also holds a ladder of ranks within itself, and its members stand one above another in a fixed and unchanging order. So one man is born to command a regiment and another a company. Once they reach the farthest goal of their hopes, they stop of their own accord and are content with their lot. In aristocracies there is, besides, a strong reason why the officer’s desire for promotion is weak. Among aristocratic nations an officer, apart from his army rank, also holds a high rank in society, and in his eyes the first is almost always just an addition to the second. A nobleman who takes up the profession of arms follows it less out of ambition than out of a sense of the duties his birth imposes on him. He joins the army to find honorable occupation for the idle years of his youth, and to bring back to his home and his peers some honorable memories of military life. But his main aim is not to gain property, distinction or power through that profession, since he already holds these advantages by right and enjoys them without leaving home.

problem: 'constitution of the people' rendered 'structure of the people', which is unnatural English and loses the sense (the nature or character of the people).
replacement: I have shown that in democratic armies in peacetime, seniority is the supreme and inflexible rule of advancement. As I noted earlier, this follows not only from the structure of these armies but from the nature of the people, and it will always be so. Also, because an officer in these nations gets his standing in the country entirely from his standing in the army, and draws from the same source all the distinction and comfortable means he enjoys, he does not leave his profession, or get retired for age, until very near the end of his life. The result of these two causes is that when a democratic people goes to war after a long stretch of peace, all the leading officers of the army are old men. I speak not only of the generals but of the non-commissioned officers, most of whom have stood still or advanced only step by step. One may notice with surprise that in a democratic army after a long peace all the soldiers are mere boys and all the senior officers are in their declining years, so that the former lack experience and the latter lack vigor. This is a strong element of defeat, for the first condition of successful generalship is youth. I would not have ventured to say so if the greatest captain of modern times had not made the observation. These two causes do not act in the same way on aristocratic armies. Men there are promoted by right of birth far more than by seniority, so at every rank there are a certain number of young men who bring to their profession the full early vigor of body and mind. Also, since the men who seek military honors among an aristocratic people hold a settled position in civil society, they seldom stay in the army until old age overtakes them. After giving the most vigorous years of their youth to the career of arms, they retire of their own accord and spend the rest of their mature years at home.
